idiom_name: static dictionary + serial DispatchQueue (or barrier writes on a concurrent queue)
implementation_notes: Swift's stored type property gives the registry a lazy, once-only, thread-safe home - the language guarantees a stored type property is initialised exactly once even when several threads reach it - but the dictionary itself is not thread-safe, so the registry is completed with a private static let DispatchQueue and every read/write of the dictionary goes through queue.sync; a concurrent queue with async(flags: .barrier) for writes is the reader-writer alternative. A private init plus a static factory keep construction closed, and the registry is per process, never shared across processes.
pitfalls: queue.sync from inside a block already running on that serial queue deadlocks - the registry queue must never re-enter, so keep the critical section free of calls back into the factory.
static let makes the registry's creation once-only, not the per-key insertion: without the queue two threads can create two entries for one key and one is silently overwritten (and leaked).
The instances dictionary retains every client forever; with per-user keys in a long-running app that is a leak, and deinit-based cleanup never runs for retained entries.
